excerpt_i18n.en: Domestic DPU company CloudLeopard Smart submitted its IPO application to the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on June 30, becoming the first DPU chip company to file under the ChiNext Board’s fourth set of listing standards, and is seen by the market as the “first domestic DPU stock.” However, after the prospectus disclosed operating data, two types of controversy emerged: net losses attributable to the parent company for three consecutive years and high revenue dependence on a single major customer. The implementation of the ChiNext Board’s fourth set of listing standards completely broke the profit requirement for listing, precisely adapting to hard-tech companies like high-end chips that require heavy upfront investment and are not yet profitable. Resolving chip bottlenecks is a core national strategic task. Among the three core computing chips in data centers, domestic substitution in the CPU and GPU tracks has achieved phased results, with local companies like Hygon, Huawei Kunpeng, Cambricon, and Huawei Ascend making continuous breakthroughs, gradually easing supply shortages. As the third key track in computing power infrastructure, DPU has long been monopolized by overseas manufacturers and is a critical link that domestic substitution in the AI industry chain urgently needs to overcome. This is also an important policy consideration behind the ChiNext Board’s fourth set of listing standards, which focuses on supporting DPU hard-tech companies like CloudLeopard Smart. On one hand, the market holds high expectations for CloudLeopard Smart’s listing as the “first DPU stock,” while on the other hand, it harbors some doubts. These doubts essentially apply the profit and customer evaluation standards of mature consumer enterprises and traditional manufacturing to high-end computing chip companies still in the early stages of commercialization. Looking at the domestic chip leaders that have already landed on the capital market, most of them experienced losses before listing.

excerpt_i18n.en: The AI short drama industry has moved beyond "wild growth" and officially entered a new phase of quality and scale. However, while most creators are still stuck in an "AI blind box" mode, three harsh realities have already emerged: uncontrollable creative processes—relying on random AI "card draws" often leads to inconsistent character appearances, shifting positions, and lack of narrative logic between shots; difficulty balancing quality and production volume—fully automated generation feels mechanical, while manual refinement cannot support large-scale delivery; and challenges in team management—multi-creator projects lack standardized tools, making it hard to unify progress tracking, computing costs, and review data.
